prose.def: To be silent or stop speaking; sometimes to keep something secret or hidden.
prose.article: σιγάω mostly means to be silent or fall quiet — to stop talking, hold one's peace, or wait without speaking. In its transitive or passive use it can also mean to keep something secret, as when Paul speaks of a mystery that was kept hidden. The word was at home in everyday Koine: a papyrus from Oxyrhynchus has an advocate demanding, "what reason had you for being silent regarding this?" In the Septuagint it renders several Hebrew words for being silent or still, including חָרַשׁ.

prose.def: The powdery residue left after something burns, especially used as a sign of mourning or repentance.
prose.article: σποδός means "ashes" — and that meaning is remarkably stable, rendered the same way in all 3 New Testament occurrences and confirmed across every source consulted. In the New Testament it appears mainly in the phrase "in sackcloth and ashes," a gesture of grief or repentance (Matthew 11:21, Luke 10:13), plus a reference to sacrificial ashes in Hebrews 9:13. In the Septuagint it translates the Hebrew word for ashes (אֵפֶר) 18 of 23 times, and everyday papyri even use a related adjective, σπόδιαι, to describe "ash-colored" or grey goats.
prose.caution: The word is rare in the New Testament (only 3 occurrences), but its meaning is consistent and undisputed across all sources.
